text:
The passage given below is followed by a set of questions. Choose the most appropriate answer to each question.

‘Shifting baseline syndrome’ names the process by which ongoing damage to the natural world is normalized over time, as each generation measures loss against an already diminished benchmark. Someone born in the 1970s may recall car windscreens spattered with insects after long journeys. Today’s windscreens bear only a fraction of those marks; yet a person born in the early 2000s would not register this as evidence of drastic ecological decline, having never known the earlier abundance. Also called ‘generational amnesia’, the effect is a powerful force, disguising degradation and enabling its continuation.

This syndrome has masked the steady ruin of rivers. Clean rivers have become rivers you cannot drink from without falling ill, which in turn have become rivers you cannot swim in without risk. Almost too late, we have woken to the scale of the catastrophe. As the river defender Feargal Sharkey has put it, ‘The simple truth of the matter is that every river in England is dying.’ They are dying through neglect, and being killed by design.

Yet decline need not be the only trajectory. Shifting baseline syndrome can operate in reverse. We might normalize recovery as readily as deterioration, and then come to desire its increase: a ‘lifting baseline syndrome’. We can run the reel backwards, imagining a future in which children expect rivers to run clear and free.

Rivers, though easily wounded, possess a remarkable capacity for self-healing when given the chance. Their life returns swiftly. When the Lower Elwha Dam in Washington State was removed in September 2011, a century after its construction, the river’s revival was breathtaking. Vast stores of sediment, long trapped behind the dam, were released to the estuary, where new flows built shingle banks and sandbars, buffering the coast and creating habitats. In the drained reservoir bed, life surged back: saplings of maple, fir and cedar; swathes of lupin; willow and cottonwood. Black bears and mountain lions moved through the regrowth. Dippers appeared, bobbing on boulders like attentive waiters.

Below the surface, further transformations unfolded. As the waters cleared and the river ran unimpeded, migrating salmon returned—first in hundreds, then thousands—driven upstream to spawn and die in the ancient cycle of the salmon run, as strange and compelling as any Greek tragedy.

With the salmon came the wider web of life. Ocean creatures by nature, they carried marine nutrients inland. Their carcasses, dragged into forests by scavengers, were broken down by fungi and absorbed into the soil, nourishing trees. By way of the river, the ocean fed the forest.

People, too, returned: hikers, families, paddlers, policymakers, and members of the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, whose sacred land had long been submerged. Having fought for decades to remove the dams, they scattered native seeds across the recovering terrain. Through such acts, the river was not only restored, but reimagined. Hope, it turns out, is the thing with rivers.

The paragraph beginning “With the salmon came the wider web of life” most directly supports the claim that:

 

A

The return of salmon mainly matters because it brings back an old and culturally important migration cycle.

B

Sea animals are mainly responsible for keeping inland ecosystems alive by bringing in nutrients.

C

When rivers recover, they naturally become balanced and self-sustaining without any further human help.

D

Restoring a river can set off a chain of effects that benefit many connected parts of the ecosystem.

Text Solution

Answer: 4

Option 1: Incorrect.
The reference to the salmon run as “the ancient cycle… as strange and compelling as any Greek tragedy” appears in the previous paragraph and emphasizes symbolic or dramatic resonance. However, the paragraph in question shifts to nutrient transfer and ecological interdependence. The claim supported is ecological interconnectedness, not cultural or mythic significance.

Option 2: Incorrect.
While the paragraph notes that salmon “carried marine nutrients inland,” it does not argue that marine species are uniquely responsible for sustaining inland ecosystems. The focus is on this specific instance of nutrient flow, not on establishing exclusivity or primacy of marine species in ecological sustenance.

Option 3: Incorrect.
The paragraph describes regenerative processes, but nowhere claims that revival “inevitably results in balanced and self-sustaining ecological systems.” Earlier, the river recovered only after the dam was removed, and people “scattered native seeds.” Thus, restoration is shown as contingent and facilitated, not automatic or inevitable.

Option 4: Correct.
The paragraph states: “With the salmon came the wider web of life.” It explains that salmon “carried marine nutrients inland,” that their “carcasses, dragged into forests by scavengers, were broken down by fungi and absorbed into the soil, nourishing trees,” and concludes, “By way of the river, the ocean fed the forest.” This chain demonstrates interconnected ecological effects extending beyond the river itself. The focus is on cascading regeneration across systems—river, ocean, forest—thus supporting the idea of interconnected restorative impact.

The correct answer is 4.

Hence, [4].
